questions.prompt: After four agents edit four files in parallel, the suite is red. You have never seen it green. What should you check first?
options: Revert all four agents' work — four simultaneous edits is always wrong
Whether the test runner is itself correct: path globs, working directory, config, and whether tests actually ran
Which agent has the most commits and start from there
Run the suite with more verbose output
questions.explanation: A red suite caused by a wrong glob looks exactly like failing code — this repo lost an afternoon to precisely that. Before concluding anything about the agents' work, confirm the runner matches real test files and actually ran tests. Verbose output is a good second step, not the first.

questions.prompt: An agent "fixed" a failing test. The error message text changed completely, but the test still fails. What has most likely happened?
options: The fix was correct; the message just got clearer
The failure was moved, not fixed — the fix needs to be proven with the identical command run before and after
The test cache is stale and needs clearing
The agent changed the test itself, which always counts as fixing
questions.explanation: A real fix changes observable behaviour, so the identical command produces a different result. Only the wording changing is the classic signature of a failure relocated rather than removed — and it will resurface somewhere less convenient.

questions.prompt: You must hand an agent a failing build. Which message gets the closest fix on the first attempt?
options: "The build is broken on the API layer, please fix it"
"Run `npm run build`. It exits 1. Verbatim output: [30 lines]. The error mentions undefined `parseHeaders` in `src/api/client.ts:88`"
"Everything worked yesterday. It doesn't work now."
"Fix the bug in the API code"
questions.explanation: An agent can only debug from evidence, and evidence is the command plus its verbatim output — which already names the file, the line and the symbol. The other three are descriptions of your feeling about the problem; the agent must reverse-engineer the facts from them, and each round trip costs a full cycle.
